tldr: Laforge and Venema define loop engineering as designing triggers, goals, checkers, state and stop conditions around coding agents, and demo maker-checker, goal, scheduled and Ralph Wiggum loops built with Antigravity.
summary: Guillaume Laforge's first loop came from frustration: Google codelabs took him two days to write. He had Antigravity turn the formatting guide into a skill, generate a codelab, compile and run every sample, then walk through the result in a fresh context and report problems, cutting the work to about two hours. Citing Boris Cherny and Peter Steinberger ('design loops that prompt your agents'), the speakers stack the vocabulary: prompt, context, harness, loop and graph engineering. A loop has a trigger, a contract (goal or standard operating procedure), a maker, a separate checker, persisted state and a stopping gate with caps.

They list six primitives: triggers (manual, schedule, events), Git worktrees, skills and rules, connectors such as MCP and A2A, sub-agents, and state files. Loops are placed on a quadrant of manual or autonomous triggers and exits: turn-based, goal-based, time-based and proactive. Laforge demos /goal to lift JaCoCo coverage above 80% one class at a time, a daily scheduled task that redeploys his Devoxx schedule app when the agenda changes, and a GitHub Action that runs a JBang script using his Antigravity Java SDK with a PR-review skill and locked-down tool policies.

Wietse Venema builds loops in Python on the Antigravity SDK, which drives the same Go harness binary as the IDE. His demos add token and tool-call budgets, output truncation and compaction (every 15,000 tokens in one run), a maker-checker where the read-only checker must find something on its first pass, a planner in front, a model-based shell command classifier as a guardrail, a 'maker-user' loop that writes friction logs from the README alone, a docs maker allowed to write only in docs/, a forced red-green-refactor TDD loop, and a 'dreaming' node that turns the maker's trajectory into a Markdown memory.

After the break, Laforge runs Geoffrey Huntley's Ralph Wiggum loop: fresh context per iteration, specs written with Matt Pocock's grill-me skill, and todo and progress files, commit only on success, building a Connect 4 game. He then walks through Andrej Karpathy's autoresearch loop, which ran 83 five-minute nanoGPT training experiments overnight and kept only improvements. Six failure modes follow: runaway token burn, unverified autonomy, uncheckable goals, impossible goals, complexity and context saturation, and away-from-keyboard comprehension rot, illustrated by a 2.0 SDK release full of Object-typed signatures. They close on graph engineering and software factories, citing Zach Lloyd of Warp, while admitting it may be 'engineers looking for engineering things'.
keyPoints: A loop's anatomy: trigger, contract (target state or SOP), maker, checker, state carried across iterations, and a stopping gate with caps on tokens, iterations or tool calls.

Never let the maker grade itself in the same conversation; use a fresh context or a different (possibly smaller) model, adversarial review prompts, and deterministic gates such as tests and linters where possible.
Goals must be checkable and reachable: asked for 100% coverage, agents have deleted hard-to-test files temporarily or added coverage ignore lists; 'make this code cleaner' has no exit condition.

Budgets matter in the harness: Venema caps tool calls per turn with a hook that warns at six of eight, truncates noisy tool output, and compacts history at a token threshold, trading lost detail against cost.

Restrict loops with policies, not just prompts: read-only checkers, docs makers that may only write to docs/, and a classifier hook on every shell command to block reads outside the workspace or calls to the cloud metadata server.
The Ralph Wiggum loop avoids context rot by restarting each iteration from scratch and keeping memory in todo/progress files and Git commits.

Karpathy's autoresearch is a roughly 600-line Python loop: hypothesise a change, train for a fixed five minutes, commit if the metric improves, otherwise reset, and log failed experiments so they are not retried.
Venema says a Google experiment found agents are often distracted by TODO comments, more so at higher thinking levels, so clear them out of codebases agents work in.
takeaways: Pick one repetitive task (release notes, doc sync, dependency updates) and turn it into a scheduled or goal-based loop with an explicit, verifiable exit condition.
Add a separate checker in a fresh context that must find at least one issue on its first pass.
Set token, iteration and tool-call caps on every autonomous loop before you walk away from it.
Persist loop state in files or Git so each iteration can start with a clean context.
Keep asking your agent to explain the code, architecture and its findings so you still understand what it built.

quotes.text: Each time you ask a model to grade itself what it has done, in the same conversation, it will always say it's good. Always.
99% of the time, it's perfectly fine. And then at one time, it does something completely unhinged.
I can't shake the feeling that this might be engineers looking for engineering things.
